title: 🍺 The History of Beer — The Liquid Bread That Created Modern Civilization
fullText: In 1814, a vat the size of a small house ruptured inside the Horseshoe Brewery in London. The vessel held over 320,000 gallons of porter, and when its iron hoop snapped, the failure set off a chain reaction. Nearby vats burst open one after another. A wall of beer roughly 15 ft high tore through the brick walls of the brewery and surged into the surrounding slum of St. Giles. Basements flooded in an instant. Houses collapsed under the pressure of the wave. Eight people drowned. Not in a river, not in the sea, but in beer. Eight people. Rescue workers spent hours waiting through sellers filled with porter, pulling bodies from the wreckage while a crowd reportedly gathered to drink the runoff pooling in the streets. It sounds almost like a joke today. A strange footnote. the kind of trivia you mention at a party. But there is one drink that built the first cities, paid the wages of the workers who raised the pyramids, and might be the reason humans learned to write in the first place. Beer. Not wine, not spirits, not some ceremonial delicacy reserved for kings. A drink you can buy for $2 a can at any gas station today was once currency, medicine, ritual offering, and quite possibly the very foundation of civilization itself. So, how did beer go from a sacred gift to the gods, a wage paid the laborers, a substance so essential that entire legal codes were built around it, to a $2 can at a gas station. That was 1814. But the story of beer starts almost 12,000 years ago in a place most people associate with bread, not beer, the fertile crescent in what is today southeastern Turkey and Iraq. Around 11,000 years ago, in the hills near a site called Gobecley, hunter gatherer communities were doing something nobody expected of people without agriculture, without permanent settlements, and without metal tools. They were fermenting grain. Archaeologists have found stone vets at Gobeclete with residues consistent with a porridge-like fermented beverage brewed from wild wheat or barley long before anyone had domesticated either crop. Think about that for a second. Some researchers now argue that the desire to brew beer, not the desire to bake bread, may have been one of the driving forces behind the domestication of grain in the first place. That theory remains debated among archaeologists and the evidence is not conclusive either way. But the fact that serious scholars are even having that argument tells you something about how central fermentation was to early human life. These early brewers did not know the word yeast. They did not know the word fermentation, let alone the microbiology behind it. They noticed that wet grain left out in the open sometimes turned bubbly, sour, and mildly intoxicating, and they kept doing it anyway. Trial, error, and an intimate understanding of their environment got them there long before science could explain why it worked. It worked. And once it worked, it never really stopped. By around 6,000 years ago, in the cities of Sumer in what is now southern Iraq, beer had stopped being an accident and became an institution. The Sumerians left behind one of the oldest pieces of writing in human history, a hymn to Ninkasi, the goddess of beer, dated to roughly 1900 years before the common era. The hymn is essentially a recipe describing the maltting, the baking of Baptier bread used as a fermentation base and the straining of the finished brew, all wrapped in religious verse. This was not a drinking song. It was a technical manual disguised as a prayer and it may be the oldest written recipe of any kind that survives today. Here is the detail that makes this strange. In a world without safe drinking water, without refrigeration, and without any concept of sanitation, beer was often safer to drink than water itself because the boiling and fermentation process killed off many of the pathogens that made untreated water dangerous. In a world like that, beer was not a luxury. It was survival. Sumerian workers were paid in beer rations, sometimes as much as 2 L a day for laborers and up to 5 L a day for higher status officials and priestesses. Beer was not an indulgence. It was payroll. There is a colorful legend attached to this era, one you will still hear repeated in documentaries and pub trivia nights alike, that beer was discovered entirely by accident when a piece of bread or a bowl of grain porridge was left out in the rain and forgotten. Now, that story is almost certainly an oversimplification, and no single accidental bowl of porridge explains a technology that spread across dozens of independent cultures within a few thousand years of each other. But the fact that some version of that origin myth exists in nearly every early brewing culture from Mesopotamia to ancient China to pre-Colombian South America tells you something important. Fermentation is not rare. It is nearly unavoidable. Leave sugary or starchy plant matter exposed to the open air for long enough and wild yeast present almost everywhere in the environment will find it. What separates a happy accident from a civilization altering technology is what happened next. The repetition, the refinement, the passing down of technique from one generation to the next. Sumerian brewers were overwhelmingly women, often priestesses attached to the temple of Nasi herself. And brewing was considered skilled, respected labor, not a domestic afterthought. This was not casual kitchen work. It was a specialized craft with its own goddess, its own hymns, and its own professional standing in one of the first literate societies on earth. The pattern repeated itself in Egypt, where beer, called hecette, was considered a gift from the god Osiris. Egyptian medical texts prescribed beer, sometimes mixed with herbs, for everything from digestive trouble to eye infections. Workers who built the pyramids at Giza, not slaves as popular Mythlong claimed, but paid laborers, were compensated in part with beer, reportedly receiving rations of up to four to 5 L a day. Four to five L of beer every single day from men hauling limestone blocks in the desert sun. That number sounds absurd by modern standards, but the beer these workers drank was thick, low in alcohol, and closer to a nutritious grl than anything you would recognize on a bar menu today. Essentially, a form of liquid bread, packed with calories and nutrients that kept exhausted laborers alive and working. This was not about getting drunk. It was about survival, nutrition, and payroll, all in a single cup. Beer even worked its way into law. The Code of Hammurabi, carved in stone in Babylon around 1750 years before the common era, includes specific regulations for tavern keepers, setting prices for beer, and prescribing harsh punishment, in some cases, death by drowning for those caught watering it down or cheating customers. Think about that. Beer fraud was at one point in human history a capital offense. Beer in ancient Egypt was not reserved for the elite either. It cut across every level of society, from pharaohs to farmers to the workers hauling stone in the desert heat. Archaeologists excavating the workers village near Giza uncovered large-scale bakeries and brewing facilities capable of producing beer on an industrial scale for their time. evidence that feeding and paying an army of laborers required something close to a coordinated food production system thousands of years before anyone had a word for logistics. Temples brewed their own beer for religious offerings. Households brewed their own for daily consumption and professional brewers sold it in markets and taverns. It was given to children in diluted form, prescribed by physicians for ailments ranging from constipation to snake bites and even included in burial goods because the dead apparently were expected to need a drink in the afterlife, too. This was not a beverage on the margins of Egyptian life. It was woven into birth, work, medicine, religion, and death all at once. This story does not stay in Mesopotamia and Egypt. It spreads north and west into Europe, carried along trade routes by Celtic and Germanic tribes who had their own long independent traditions of fermenting grain. But the story of beer gets bigger and stranger once it collides with medieval Europe, where an entirely different institution took over the brewing tradition, the monastery. Throughout the early medieval period, monasteries across what is now Germany, Belgium, and France became centers of brewing knowledge. Not despite their religious mission, but partly because of it. Monks needed something safe to drink during long fasting periods, and beer being liquid was technically permitted even under strict fasting rules that banned solid food. Some monastic brews were reportedly strong enough that monks referred to them informally as liquid bread, a drink hardy enough to sustain a man through weeks of fasting. Monasteries also had something almost no one else in medieval Europe had. Literacy, stability, and the ability to preserve and refine recipes across generations. While the rest of Europe brewed beer that varied wildly in quality and safety, monasteries were quietly running what amounted to the first standardized breweries in Western history. Some monasteries even brewed multiple grades of beer at once. A weaker, thinner brew for daily drinking by lay workers and a stronger, richer brew reserved for monks, pilgrims, and honored guests. Essentially running a tiered production line centuries before anyone used that phrase. Pilgrims traveling long distances between religious sites relied on monasteries not just for shelter and prayer but for a safe calorie dense drink to sustain them on the road which meant that monastic beer functioned as something close to medieval travel infrastructure. The word beer itself likely traces back to the Latin bare meaning to drink filtered through old English and old fian before settling into the word we use today. A reminder that for most of European history, this drink was simply understood as drink itself. Not one option among many. For most of this era, European beer was flavored and preserved not with hobbs, but with a mixture of herbs and spices called gruit, which could include anything from bog myrtle to yrow to juniper. Gruit was not just a flavoring. It was a monopoly. In many regions, local bishops and nobles held exclusive rights to sell gruit, which meant they effectively controlled the beer supply of entire towns and taxed it heavily. This was not about seasoning beer. Gruit rights were a revenue stream for the church in the aristocracy, baked directly into the price of every mug sold. That began to change with the introduction of hops as a primary bittering and preservative agent. A shift that took hold gradually across German-speaking regions. Starting around the 12th century, [snorts] hops did something Grruit could not do particularly well. They acted as a natural preservative, extending the shelf life of beer and making it possible to transport over longer distances without spoiling. And here is the detail that makes this strange. Because hops broke the Grruit monopoly, the shift toward hopped beer was in part a quiet economic revolt against the church's control over the drink of ordinary people. This was not just a change in flavor. It was a redistribution of power. The transition was not instant, and it was not peaceful either. Regions that clung to grrew taxation fought hard to protect it, sometimes banning hopped beer outright or taxing it punitively to protect the older monopoly. Merchants and brewers who wanted to use hops instead had to petition, smuggle, or simply wait out local rulers who had every financial incentive to keep Gruitit alive as long as possible. Slowly hop growing regions in northern Germany in the low countries gained an economic edge because hopped beer traveled and kept better which meant it could be exported for profit in a way grew it beer more prone to spoiling generally could not. By the 14 and 1500s hopped beer had become the dominant style across most of Northern Europe and English brewers who had resisted the hop for generations in favor of their own unhopped ale tradition eventually adopted it as well. if only because hopped beer from the continent kept out competing them on shelf life and price. Tradition lost to logistics. It usually does. By the time hops had become dominant across much of Europe, beer had also become the everyday drink of ordinary people in a way wine never was. Largely because barley grew far more easily than grape vines in the cooler climates of Northern Europe. In England, in Germany, in the low countries, beer was not a special occasion drink. It was breakfast. Weak, lowalcohol beer, sometimes called small beer, was routinely given to children because it was once again safer than the local water supply. This is where the story takes a turn nobody expected. Because in 1616 in the city of Munich, a Duke named William IVth of Bavaria signed a decree that would end up shaping beer more than almost any single document in history. Now that document, the Reinhit Scabat, is usually dated to 1516 and it stated in essence that beer sold in Bavaria could legally contain only three ingredients: water, barley, and hops. Yeast was not included simply because at the time nobody understood that yeast was a living organism responsible for fermentation. That knowledge would not arrive for more than 300 years. The Rin Heights Kabat was framed partly as consumer protection, preventing brewers from cutting their beer with cheaper, sometimes dangerous additives like soot or toxic herbs to stretch their profits. But it was also quite bluntly about protecting the price and supply of wheat and rye for bread by restricting brewers to barley alone. This was not purely about purity. It was about food security and political control wrapped in the language of quality. Whether every detail of the traditional story around its passage is fully accurate remains debated among historians, but the law's influence is beyond dispute. It became one of the oldest food regulations still referenced in food production anywhere in the world, and versions of it still shape how beer is legally defined in Germany today. Beer, by this point, had also become deeply entangled with taxation and guild politics across much of Europe. In England, brewing guilds controlled who could legally sell beer within city walls, while monarchs repeatedly imposed and raised excise taxes on beer and malt to fund wars, palaces, and eventually entire colonial ventures. This was not incidental revenue. In many European states, beer and malt taxes became one of the single largest sources of government income for centuries, funding armies that never touched a drop of the beer that paid for them. Brewers who tried to evade these taxes faced fines, confiscation, or worse, and smuggling watered down or untacked beer became its own quiet criminal economy running parallel to the legitimate trade. Pay attention to this next detail because it explains a pattern that repeats throughout beer's entire history. Almost every time beer becomes valuable enough to tax, control, or monopolize, someone in power finds a way to use that control for something far bigger than beer itself. If you are finding this interesting, hit subscribe. We cover stories like this every week, and you will not want to miss what comes next. Because Beer's story is about to turn from clever laws and monastery brewing into something much darker. Because for every story of monks and dukes and clever laws, there is a parallel history of exploitation, addiction, and control. One that rarely makes it into the trivia nights. Beer and alcohol more broadly became one of the most effective tools of colonial administration in 19th and 20th century Africa. And nowhere is that clearer than in South Africa. Under colonial and later apartheid governments, municipal authorities in South African cities established a system of state controlled beer halls in black urban townships where the sale of traditional sorghum beer known as um kombotei was made a municipal monopoly. Black residents were for extended periods legally barred from brewing or selling their own beer, forcing them to buy it instead from government-run beer halls at prices set by the state. Here is the uncomfortable part. The profits from these beer hall monopolies were used to fund the very administrative apparatus of segregation, including township policing and municipal enforcement of the past laws that restricted black South Africans movement. Beer did not just generate revenue. Beer helped bankroll the machinery of racial control. This was not a side effect. It was policy. Women in these townships organized repeated boycots and protests against the beer halls throughout the 1920s,30s, and beyond precisely because they understood what the system was funding. Some of the most sustained resistance to this system came from black women who were largely excluded from formal wage labor under the colonial and apartheid economy and had traditionally brewed and sold beer independently as one of the few sources of income available to them. The municipal beer hall monopolies directly threatened that livelihood, which is part of why women led repeated, sometimes violent protests against the beer halls across South African townships for decades, including major demonstrations in the 1920s and again in the 1950s. These were not minor local disputes. They were sustained acts of economic and political resistance fought over the right to brew and sell a drink that the state had turned into an instrument of control. This is the part that should make you angry and it is a piece of beer's history that almost never makes it into a pub trivia night. Beer's darker chapters were not confined to the colonial world. In the United States, growing alarm over alcohol social costs fueled by temperance movements, religious campaigns, and genuine public health concerns about domestic violence and poverty linked to heavy drinking culminated in the ratification of the 18th Amendment and the passage of the Volstead Act, ushering in nationwide prohibition beginning in 1920. For 13 years, the legal production and sale of beer in America virtually vanished overnight. Major breweries including giants like Annheiser Bush and Paps were forced to pivot to other products just to survive. Brewing near beer, malt syrup, ice cream, and even truck bodies to keep their factories running. But prohibition did not eliminate the demand for beer. It simply pushed it underground. And that vacuum was filled by organized crime on a scale America had never seen. Bootlegging operations, illegal breweries, and speak easys became enormously profitable, fueling the rise of figures like Al Capone, whose criminal empire in Chicago was built substantially on illegal alcohol distribution. This was not a victory for public health. It was a redirection of an entire industry into the hands of criminal syndicates, and it took the death of countless people in gang violence and from poisoned, unregulated bootleg liquor before the country reversed course. Prohibition was repealed in 1933, and the legal beer industry that emerged afterward looked nothing like the fragmented, locally rooted brewing culture that had existed before it. It emerged smaller, more consolidated, and dominated by the handful of large breweries that had the resources to survive over a decade without legally selling their core product. Of the roughly 1,300 breweries operating in the United States just before prohibition began, only a few hundred reopened once it ended. And of those, an even smaller number would survive the next several decades of consolidation intact. The human cost of prohibition rarely gets mentioned alongside the gangster mythology. Because legal alcohol production had vanished, some bootleggers turned to industrial alcohol meant for fuel and manufacturing and attempted to redistill it for drinking, sometimes without fully removing the toxic additives the government had specifically ordered added to industrial alcohol to discourage exactly this practice. Historians estimate that thousands of Americans died from drinking poisoned bootleg liquor over the course of prohibition, a policy failure so severe that it helped turn public opinion decisively against the entire experiment. This was not a story about beer becoming dangerous. It was a story about what happens when demand for something people consider essential collides headon with a law trying to erase it overnight. That consolidation only accelerated once science caught up with what brewers had been doing blindly for thousands of years. In the 1860s, the French chemist Louie Pastor, while investigating why French beer and wine kept spoiling in ways that frustrated domestic brewers competing with English exports, discovered that fermentation was driven by living microorganisms, yeast, rather than a purely chemical process. This was not a minor academic curiosity. It was the missing piece that explained everything monks and Sumerian priestesses had been doing for millennia without understanding why. Pastor went on to develop the heat treatment process that still bears his name, pasteurization, which allowed brewers to kill off unwanted bacteria and dramatically extend the shelf life of beer, making it possible for the first time to ship beer over long distances without it spoiling into vinegar along the way. Around the same period in 1842, a young brewer named Joseph Gro, working in the Bohemian town of Pilzen in what is now the Czech Republic, combined pale maltted barley, soft local water, and saw hops to create a golden, clear, crisp logger unlike anything most drinkers had ever seen. Beer before this point had almost universally been dark, cloudy, and often inconsistent. Gro's creation, Pzner, was pale gold and brilliantly clear, and it triggered a wave of imitation across Europe, so widespread that the word Pzner became merely synonymous with logger itself. None of this happened without cost to the people doing the actual work. 19th century industrial breweries were loud, dangerous places full of scalding vats, heavy machinery, and grain dust thick enough to occasionally ignite. Brewery workers labored long shifts in extreme heat near boiling mash tons and serious injuries, burns, crushed limbs from malfunctioning machinery were common enough that early labor organizing in cities like Milwaukee and St. Louis found some of its earliest footholds inside brewery walls. The industry that would eventually market itself with cheerful jingles about friendship and refreshment was in its formative decades built on genuinely brutal working conditions. Combine Pastor's preservation science with the invention of industrial refrigeration in the late 19th century and something remarkable happened. Beer for the first time in human history could be brewed consistently, shipped over enormous distances and stored for months without spoiling. That combination is more than almost any single factor why a handful of massive industrial breweries came to dominate global beer production over the following century. This decision to industrialize and consolidate seemed at the time like simple progress. It was not, at least not for the thousands of small local breweries that could not compete with companies who could now brew millions of barrels a year and ship them across continents. In the United States alone, the number of breweries collapsed from more than 4,000 in the years before Prohibition to only a few dozen dominant national players by the midentth century. Meanwhile, the technology kept accelerating. The first commercially canned beer was sold by the Krueger Brewing Company in New Jersey in 1935, and the format proved wildly popular, being lighter, more portable, and more resistant to light damage than glass bottles. Combine that with the rise of national advertising, radio jingles, and later television commercials, and beer transformed once again. This time from a regional, almost artisal product into a nationally branded mass-marketed consumer good sold the same way as soap or cigarettes. Which brings the story to today. And the scale here genuinely takes people by surprise. Global beer production now exceeds roughly 1.9 billion hectalers a year. An amount so large it is almost impossible to visualize. But picture roughly 750 Olympic size swimming pools filled entirely with beer produced every single year. China is currently the single largest beer producing nation on Earth, followed by the United States and Brazil. And the global beer market is valued at several hundred billion dollar annually. But raw scale is not even the strangest part of beer's modern story. That would be the curveball because beer is far more than just a beverage. And this next part tends to catch people off guard. The spent grain left over after brewing, the solid barley residue strained out after mashing, is not simply thrown away. It is routinely repurposed as high protein animal feed for cattle, pigs, and poultry, turning what could be an enormous waist stream into a genuinely valuable agricultural byproduct. Brewer's yeast, the very organism Pastor identified a century and a half ago, is harvested and sold as a nutritional supplement rich in B vitamins and shows up in everything from health food store shelves to hangover cure marketing. Beer has been used quite literally as an ingredient in shampoos and hair conditioners, marketed on the claim that the proteins in hops and malt can add shine and body to hair. And here is the detail that should genuinely surprise you. Astronauts aboard research missions and private space companies have experimented with brewing beer in microgravity partly as a genuine scientific study of how fermentation behaves without gravity and partly frankly because the question of whether you can drink a beer in space is exactly the kind of thing scientists cannot resist testing. Not bad for a drink whose most famous historical use was paying pyramid builders in the desert. Here is another detail that tends to catch people offguard. Beer's byproducts have quietly become part of renewable energy research as well, with several breweries around the world experimenting with converting leftover waste water and spent yeast into bio gas, capturing methane that would otherwise simply escape into the atmosphere and using it to help power the very brewing facilities that produced it. A handful of large breweries have installed on-site bio gas plants capable of covering a meaningful share of their own energy needs, turning what used to be pure waste disposal costs into a partial energy solution. And on the more whimsical end of things, several major breweries have run high-profile publicity experiments testing how beer fermentss, tastes, and behaves after being aged at extreme depths underwater, or in a few documented cases sent briefly to the edge of space and back. Less about producing a commercially viable product and more about generating headlines. Though the underlying fermentation science involved is genuine. Even the humble pretzel, so commonly paired with beer in German beer gardens, has a plausible connection back to monastic life, with some food historians tracing its twisted shape to monks folding dough to resemble arms crossed in prayer. A detail that, however charming, remains disputed among culinary historians rather than settled fact. Meanwhile, the beer industry itself keeps splitting in two very different directions at once. On one side, a small handful of multinational conglomerates formed through decades of mergers and acquisitions now control an enormous share of global beer production and distribution. On the other side, a craft brewing renaissance has exploded since the 1980s, particularly in the United States, where the number of breweries has climbed from roughly fewer than 100 in the late 1970s to well over 9,000 today, as small independent brewers reclaimed some of the local experimental character that industrialization had spent a century smoothing away. And in a twist that would have baffled a Sumerian priestess pouring beer rations for pyramid laborers, one of the fastest growing segments of the entire modern beer market is non-alcoholic beer. As healthconscious drinkers seek out the flavor and ritual of beer without the alcohol itself, essentially reinventing, whether they realize it or not, something closer to the mild, nutrient-rich small beer that medieval children once drank at breakfast because it was safer than the water. Meanwhile, per capita consumption tells its own quiet story about how differently the world still drinks. Some central European countries, particularly the Czech Republic, consistently report the highest per capita beer consumption on the planet with average annual consumption figures reported at well over 100 L per person. a number that dwarfs consumption levels in most of the rest of the world and a fairly direct cultural inheritance from that same bohemian brewing tradition that gave the world pillzner nearly two centuries ago. Compare that to countries where religious or cultural norms limit or prohibit alcohol entirely, and you get a global map of beer consumption that still in its own way traces the outlines of history, religion, and economics layered on top of each other for thousands of years. It was there in the earliest fermenting vats of the fertile crescent more than 11,000 years ago, possibly before humans had even fully domesticated the grain it was made from. It was there in Sumer, written into humanity's oldest surviving hymns and recipes. It was there in Egypt, paying the wages of the men who built the pyramids. It was there in the code of Hammurabi, backed by the threat of death for anyone who dared water it down. It was there in medieval monasteries, sustaining monks through weeks of religious fasting. It was there in the political fight over Grruit monopolies and in the quiet revolution that Hops brought when they broke those monopolies apart. It was there in a Bavarian duke's decree that still shapes food law 5 centuries later. It was there weaponized in the beer halls of apartheid era South Africa funding the machinery of segregation. It was there when American prohibition handed an entire industry to organized crime. And it was there again when the industry rebuilt itself leaner and more consolidated in prohibition's aftermath. It was there when a French chemist finally explained scientifically what brewers had been doing by instinct for thousands of years. And it is there right now in your refrigerator, in a gas station cooler, in a can that costs less than a cup of coffee, carrying inside it 11,000 years of gods, wages, wars, laws, exploitation, and reinvention. Beer is never just beer. It never was. If any part of this surprised you, let me know in the comments which piece of beer's history you did not expect. And if you enjoyed this one, do me a favor and hit subscribe because we have a lot more stories like this coming. And I will see you in the next one.

Con tàu chứa hơn 320.000 gallon chất khuân vác, và khi vòng sắt của nó bị gãy, sự thất bại đã gây ra một phản ứng dây chuyền. Các thùng gần đó lần lượt mở ra. Một bức tường bia cao khoảng 15 ft xé toạc bức tường gạch của nhà máy bia và tiến vào khu ổ chuột xung quanh St. Giles. Tầng hầm ngập nước ngay lập tức. Những ngôi nhà đổ sập dưới sức ép của sóng. Nhưng có một loại đồ uống đã xây dựng nên những thành phố đầu tiên, trả mức lương những người công nhân đã xây dựng các kim tự tháp và có thể là lý do khiến con người học cách viết ngay từ đầu. Beer. Không phải rượu, không phải rượu mạnh, không phải món ngon nghi lễ nào đó dành riêng cho các vị vua. Vậy làm thế nào mà bia lại từ một món quà thiêng liêng dâng lên các vị thần, một món lương trả cho người lao động, một nội dung thiết yếu đến mức toàn bộ bộ luật pháp được xây dựng xung quanh nó, đến một lon 2 đô la tại một trạm xăng. Đó là năm 1814. Nhưng câu chuyện về bia bắt đầu gần 12.000 năm trước ở một nơi mọi người liên tưởng đến bánh mì chứ không phải bia, vùng lưỡi liềm màu mỡ ở vùng đông nam ngày nay Thổ Nhĩ Kỳ và Iraq. Khoảng 11.000 năm trước, trên những ngọn đồi gần địa điểm có tên Gobecley, thợ săn hái lượm cộng đồng đang làm điều mà không ai mong đợi ở những người không có nông nghiệp, không có khu định cư lâu dài và không có dụng cụ kim loại. Họ đang lên men ngũ cốc. Các nhà khảo cổ học đã tìm thấy những tấm bia đá ở Gobeclete có dấu vết phù hợp với một loại chất lên men giống như cháo đồ uống được ủ từ lúa mì hoặc lúa mạch hoang dã từ rất lâu trước khi có người thuần hóa cả hai loại cây trồng này.
